B14_00: Immune defence in blood and tissues, concerning the restraint that keeps a rapidly amplifying blood-borne defence system aimed at pathogens rather than the body's own cells. Losing these brakes causes hereditary angioedema and destruction of red blood cells, as in paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria. The same restraint marks host cells as off-limits, shaping tolerance, clearance of dying cells and inflammation in kidney, eye and blood.
B14_01: The brain's ability to filter redundant sensory input, measured by how a weak warning stimulus reduces the startle reflex to a loud one. This sensorimotor gating is consistently impaired in schizophrenia, autism and Tourette syndrome and is the standard laboratory test of antipsychotic drug action. It reflects the function of striatal circuits and their neurodevelopmental wiring.
B14_02: The developing nervous system, where growing axons are steered away from wrong destinations so that they turn, stall or prune incorrect branches. This repulsive guidance builds the correct wiring diagram, including topographic maps, midline crossings and tract boundaries. Its loss produces misrouted projections, defective commissures and abnormal sensory and olfactory targeting, and the same cues later limit nerve regrowth after adult injury.
B14_03: Cells under endoplasmic reticulum stress, particularly secretory cells, concerning how one branch of the stress response is switched off once protein folding recovers. Ending the response at the right time avoids cell death caused by chronic signalling. This balance determines whether stress resolves adaptively or kills the cell, which is relevant to secretory cell function, metabolic disease and neurodegeneration.
B14_04: The immune system's defence against intracellular pathogens, concerning the brakes on Th1 type responses. Such responses clear infection but, unchecked, cause tissue damage and autoimmunity. Loss of restraint underlies chronic inflammatory disease, whereas excessive restraint within tumours blunts protective antitumour T cell activity, a consideration for cancer immunotherapy.
B14_05: Cytotoxic T cells that kill infected and cancerous cells, concerning the brakes that spare healthy tissue and allow immune responses to resolve. The same protection is used at the maternal-fetal interface to prevent attack on the fetus and is exploited by tumours and viruses to escape clearance. Too little restraint contributes to autoimmunity and transplant rejection; too much allows tumour and viral persistence.
B14_06: Inflammation driven by a major pro-inflammatory cytokine, concerning the brakes that limit how strongly and how long the response runs. Persistent signalling underlies chronic inflammatory disease, metabolic dysfunction and tissue destruction, whereas excessive braking permits infection and tumour survival. Signals from fat tissue, plasma lipoproteins and liver bile handling feed into this control, linking it to metabolic disease.
B14_07: Blood vessels, concerning the brakes on directed migration of the endothelial cells lining them. This restraint keeps established vessels quiescent, limits excessive sprouting during wound repair and forms part of the body's natural resistance to tumour angiogenesis. When these brakes are lost, vessels grow in a disorganised and leaky fashion, relevant to cancer, wound healing and tissue remodelling.
B14_08: Helper T cells of the immune system, concerning restraint of their commitment to the Th2 lineage that orchestrates type 2 immunity. Unchecked, this lineage drives allergic inflammation, asthma, atopy and eosinophilia. Restraint keeps type 2 immunity proportionate to parasite and barrier challenges and allows alternative helper fates, such as those supporting antibody responses in lymphoid follicles.
B14_09: Blood vessel growth, concerning how strongly endothelial cells respond to a key growth signal so that angiogenesis stays proportionate rather than runaway. This restraint maintains vascular quiescence in adult tissues and supports orderly vessel patterning in wounds and the retina. Its loss contributes to tumour vascularisation and proliferative retinopathy, and immune signals add an antiangiogenic influence.
B14_10: Embryonic development and adult tissue growth, concerning brakes on a growth factor receptor family that drives proliferation, patterning and branching of organs. This restraint keeps limb, skeletal, lung and kidney development within bounds and limits blood vessel growth. Its loss contributes to developmental disorders and to cancers in which these receptor pathways are amplified or mutated.
B14_11: Inflammation and immunity, concerning the damping of a cytokine that drives acute-phase responses, fever and the development of Th17 and antibody-secreting cells. Unchecked, this signal sustains chronic inflammation and contributes to rheumatoid arthritis, cytokine storm and inflammation-associated cancer. The braking arm helps inflammation resolve once it has done its work rather than blocking it outright.
B14_12: Innate immunity, concerning brakes on the recruitment of monocytes from blood into sites of injury and infection. Limiting their influx reduces damage from prolonged inflammation and shapes how atherosclerotic lesions, fibrotic scars and healing wounds develop, since each depends on how many monocyte-derived macrophages arrive. It restrains immune cell trafficking rather than only the production of attracting signals.
B14_13: Activated T cells, concerning restraint of how much signalling cytokine they produce. Dampening this output limits collateral tissue damage during infection and enforces peripheral tolerance, and tumours exploit it to blunt local immunity. Loss of this restraint produces autoimmunity and cytokine-driven inflammatory disease, exemplified by the severe multi-organ autoimmunity of IPEX syndrome, in which regulatory T cells fail.
B14_14: Blood vessels, concerning brakes on endothelial cell responses to the main angiogenic signal. This restraint sets how much vessel sprouting, leakiness and endothelial proliferation a tissue undergoes and keeps established vessels quiescent. Its loss contributes to excessive or disorganised angiogenesis in tumours, retinopathy and vascular malformations, making it relevant to anti-angiogenic therapy.
B14_15: Innate immunity, concerning brakes on the recruitment of neutrophils and eosinophils to infected or damaged tissue. Restraint allows granulocyte influx to resolve rather than destroy the tissue it should protect. Its loss favours persistent neutrophilic inflammation of the kind seen in sepsis, arthritis and chronic lung disease, linking inflammation resolution to leukocyte trafficking.
B14_16: Cells under endoplasmic reticulum stress, concerning how they restore normal protein production after a stress-induced shutdown. Ending the response appropriately avoids commitment to cell death when stress is transient. Loss of this braking leaves cells chronically unable to make proteins, while excessive braking lets folding stress go unchecked, a balance that matters in secretory tissues and in metabolic and neurodegenerative disease.
B14_17: Tissue repair and homeostasis, concerning how cells limit their response to a major profibrotic growth factor. Restraint prevents fibrosis and excessive scarring and limits the tumour-promoting effects of the signal, notably in fibroblasts and kidney mesangial cells. Loss of restraint contributes to organ fibrosis, while excessive restraint removes the normal growth-limiting protection in epithelia, which can favour cancer.
B14_18: Cells under heavy protein-folding load, notably pancreatic beta cells, plasma cells and osteoblasts, concerning how much stress they can tolerate before dying. Loss of this protective capacity causes cell death and diabetes, as in Wolfram syndrome. It also links stress tolerance to neuronal survival, connecting to Parkinson disease and optic nerve degeneration.
B14_19: Blood vessel walls, where smooth muscle cells normally stay quiescent within the middle layer. This restraint blocks their migration into the inner layer, which drives vessel narrowing after angioplasty, transplant vasculopathy and the fibrous cap of atherosclerotic plaque. Losing it allows cells to switch to a migratory, synthetic state, so the process opposes harmful vascular remodelling after injury.
B14_20: Skeletal development, joint formation, blood vessel development and body iron balance, all governed by a family of bone-forming growth signals that must be switched off precisely. Loss of this restraint produces heterotopic ossification and sclerosing bone disease. One branch controls how the liver regulates iron absorption, so defects also cause systemic iron overload or iron-refractory anaemia.
B14_21: Antibody-driven immune defence in the blood, concerning the brakes that aim destruction at pathogens rather than host tissue and keep antibody responses in proportion. Failure underlies atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, age-related macular degeneration and lupus-like autoimmunity. Some pathogens and tumour cells exploit these brakes to evade destruction, and B cells and myeloid cells use them to avoid overreacting to immune complexes.
B14_22: Immune cell trafficking, concerning when migrating leukocytes stop responding to attracting gradients, which limits inflammatory infiltration and keeps cells from overshooting their targets. Loss of this restraint favours persistent inflammatory cell recruitment. The same biology also affects neurons and tumour cells, linking leukocyte migration to nervous system wiring and blood vessel patterning.
B14_23: Helper T cells of the immune system, concerning restraint of commitment to the Th17 lineage. These cells drive neutrophilic inflammation and are implicated in psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease and other autoimmune conditions, so their numbers must be capped once a response is underway. The process belongs to T cell development and peripheral tolerance rather than to effector function.
B14_24: Innate immunity, concerning brakes on the recruitment of macrophages to sites of injury or infection and on how far they travel once there. Without such restraint, inflammatory infiltrates persist and cause collateral tissue damage. Sex hormone status influences the strength of this restraint, one route by which sex differences shape inflammation and the resolution phase of wound healing.
B14_25: The endoplasmic reticulum of secretory and other cells, concerning limits on the disposal of misfolded or regulated proteins. Damping disposal gives slow-folding but functional proteins a chance to mature and allows regulated proteins to be tuned rather than destroyed. Loss of this restraint accelerates turnover, and one component links the process to the integrity of the kidney proximal tubule.
